13.0.0.en: Samuel wrote this verse three years after the anointing of Saul as king, and he makes clear to us in this verse that Saul was anointed king and remained for a year until he was crowned and declared king to the people at Mizpah (ch. 10:24). During the two years after the first year his kingdom was established, especially after his victory over the Ammonites and his being declared king at Gilgal (ch. 11:14). There is another opinion that during the first year he was crowned and was victorious over the Ammonites and all the people submitted to him, and then in the following two years he organized the kingdom and began to prepare the army.

13.1.0.en: Michmash: located about 8 km north of Jerusalem, and it has the same name today.

13.1.1.en: Mount Bethel: the hill country at Bethel, which lies east of Jerusalem, midway between it and Nablus.

13.1.2.en: Gibeah of Benjamin: north of Jerusalem and about 1.5 km south of Michmash; the meaning of Gibeah is “hill.”

13.1.3.en: About twenty years passed between this verse and the previous verse, in which Saul, who was a young man when he was anointed (1 Sam 9:2), grew older and had a young son, Jonathan. It seems that he organized the kingdom during the twenty years, and perhaps a weakness occurred in the army, so he organized his army anew, placing two thousand soldiers with him at Michmash and the other company, numbering a thousand, with his son Jonathan at Gibeah of Benjamin.

13.2.0.en: The garrison of the Philistines: the camp of the Philistines.

13.2.1.en: Geba: located about 9.5 km east of Jerusalem. The meaning of Geba is “hill.”

13.2.2.en: The Philistines often occupied some Israelite villages or hillsides and would set up a camp in the middle of the land to establish their presence. Their camping at Geba, which is in the tribe of Benjamin, and Saul’s slackness in driving them out from there, was due to his preoccupation with kingship, his personal glories and his comfort, so he neglected their presence inside his own tribe. This is a symbol of a person’s neglecting the presence of sin within him and being occupied with his many interests, so that it can corrupt him and destroy him.

13.2.3.en: Jonathan, who had become a young man, took notice, and he rose with the thousand men and made a raid on one of the camps of the Philistines and prevailed over them. The matter naturally reached the rest of the Philistines and also Saul, and for this reason Saul expected a retaliatory attack from the Philistines, so he blew the trumpet, proclaiming in all the tribes the necessity of the people gathering around him.

13.3.0.en: Israel had become a stench: Israel had become hated by the Philistines.

13.3.1.en: The news reached all the people that Saul had smitten the camp of the Philistines (the one meant here, of course, is his son Jonathan), and it also became known to all that the Philistines were enraged because of what had befallen them and were preparing for war. So the men of the people gathered with King Saul at Gilgal for war, to support Jonathan in the face of the many armies of the Philistines.

13.4.0.en: Beth-aven: located between Bethel to the west and Michmash to the east, and it means “house of idols.”

13.4.1.en: In a way not seen before, the Philistines gathered with a great army from all their cities. The army consisted of thirty thousand chariots, some of them war chariots used in fighting, some carrying supplies, and others used for the lodging and sleeping of the commanders, as well as six thousand horsemen skilled in fighting and a countless number of men. They drew near and encamped before Michmash, which was the town Saul had taken as a base for his men (v. 2), and by this the Philistines separated the army that was with Saul from the army that was with Jonathan, so that Jonathan could not come to his father’s aid.

13.5.1.en: Caves: plural of cave, a hollow like a cavern in the belly of a mountain, suitable for hiding.

13.5.2.en: Thickets: a place like a marsh, with water that is not deep, containing some trees and tall grasses.

13.5.3.en: High places: plural of a high place, a large, strong building suitable for taking shelter in.

13.5.4.en: Before these huge numbers of the Philistines, the people gathered around Saul were terrified, so they fled and hid in the caves and among the trees growing in the thickets, and others in the high places, and some went down into deep, dry pits, because of the weakness of their faith. It would have been better for them to pray to God to rescue them.

13.6.0.en: Many of the men of Israel also slipped away to the eastern side of the Jordan River, where the lands of the tribe of Gad and some of the Gileadites are. As for Saul, he felt all this and saw that the frightened people were dispersing and going away from around him.

13.7.0.en: We understand from this verse that when Samuel learned of the people’s gathering behind Saul at Gilgal, he had given him an appointment to come after seven days to offer his sacrifices and bless the people before the battle, but it seems that he was late for his appointment, and the people had begun to slip away from behind Saul.

13.8.0.en: With Samuel’s delay and Saul’s fear that the rest of the men would leave him, his soul was distressed and he lost his wisdom, and he decided to do a work that was not his to do, which was to offer by himself the sacrifices and the burnt offering to God ... the work that God assigned only to the priests.

13.8.1.en: There are two important lessons, beloved. The first lesson we learn from the frightened people who slipped away in flight, for they looked at the strength of the enemy (Satan) and forgot God’s former works with them, which never depended on number or equipment ... This is what happens to us often, and it makes us look for human methods in facing evil and forget our God who is able to do all things.

13.8.2.en: The second lesson is Saul’s mistake: however great the distress or anxiety, you must not, in your tension, transgress against God in one of His important commands, as Saul did by offering the sacrifice.

13.8.3.en: (2) Samuel rebukes Saul (vv. 10-15): 10 And it came to pass, that as soon as he had made an end of offering the burnt offering, behold, Samuel came; and Saul went out to meet him, that he might bless him. 11 And Samuel said, What hast thou done? And Saul said, Because I saw that the people were scattered from me, and that thou camest not within the days appointed, and that the Philistines gathered themselves together at Michmash; 12 Therefore said I, The Philistines will come down now upon me to Gilgal, and I have not made supplication unto the LORD: I forced myself therefore, and offered a burnt offering. 13 And Samuel said to Saul, Thou hast done foolishly: thou hast not kept the commandment of the LORD thy God, which he commanded thee: for now would the LORD have established thy kingdom upon Israel for ever. 14 But now thy kingdom shall not continue: the LORD hath sought him a man after his own heart, and the LORD hath commanded him to be captain over his people, because thou hast not kept that which the LORD commanded thee. 15 And Samuel arose, and gat him up from Gilgal unto Gibeah of Benjamin. And Saul numbered the people that were present with him, about six hundred men.

13.9.0.en: Samuel came to Gilgal, but Saul had finished slaughtering and offering the burnt offering, and when Saul saw him he went out to meet him and welcome him and to receive the blessing from him.

13.10.0.en: Samuel knew that Saul had offered a burnt offering, whether from its traces, or because the people told him, or because he knew it by the Spirit of God who was in him, so he took the initiative with a direct question to Saul about what he had done. Because the question was stern, Saul began to justify his act, offering excuses first before answering Samuel about what he had done. His arguments were that Samuel was late for his appointment, that the people had slipped away and dispersed from around him, and that the Philistines were encamped at Michmash, and he feared that the Philistines would attack him at Gilgal before he prayed to God and offered the sacrifices, and for this reason he took courage and offered the burnt offering. This shows Saul’s pride, which made him presume and do the works of the priesthood; and when Samuel confronted him with what he had done, he did not repent and grieve but justified his error. We notice here a group of mistakes that Saul committed, which are:

13.10.1.en: 1- His neglect to receive Samuel’s blessing, contrary to what he did at the beginning of his wars when he was victorious over the Ammonites (ch. 11:7).

13.10.2.en: 2- In pride and slackness he usurped the right of the priesthood and offered the sacrifice, although he was not a priest, since he considered the offering of the sacrifice a formality, and, being king, why should he not do it, for the position of king is very great.

13.10.3.en: 3- His neglect of the continual preparation of the army in the previous years, so that the Philistines moved and seized some of the lands and set up camps for themselves while he was heedless, preoccupied with himself as king.

13.10.4.en: 4- In pride he rebuked Samuel for his delay, in order to cover his error and justify himself.

13.10.5.en: 5- When Samuel rebuked him, he did not repent from his heart because he did not feel all his former errors.

13.11.0.en: All these excuses were not sufficient or a justification for the great error Saul committed by offering the burnt offering when he was not a priest, and for this reason the words of Samuel (which were from God) to Saul were stern and harsh. He first described him as foolish and rash, and said that he had broken the commandments and laws of the Lord concerning the person who offers the sacrifice, for he must be a priest, and that by this he had exposed himself to God’s rejection of him. God had promised to establish Saul’s kingdom, and that the kingdom and its kings from his seed would endure for ever, but because of this grave error, God would take the kingdom and the rule away from his seed. Moreover, God would raise up another man from the people, according to His own choice, whose deeds would be pleasing before God, and he would reign over the people in place of Saul, who did not keep God’s commandments. The reference here was of course to David the prophet, the coming king of Israel, and Samuel knew this by the spirit of prophecy and spoke of the events in the past tense because what God has decided must come to pass.

13.11.1.en: Samuel’s words are the carrying out of the prophecy of Jacob, who declared in his prophecy to his sons that the kingship would belong to the tribe of Judah, from which David came (Gen 49). Therefore Saul’s kingship was temporary and a preparation for the true king, who is David, and from whose seed Christ would come. Saul is considered a king in form, but a preparation for the true king. The same meaning was repeated at the birth of Christ among the Jews: His descent from them according to the flesh is the beginning, but the truth is that those who believed in Him most were the Gentiles. He is King over the children of Israel according to the flesh, but He reigns spiritually over the Gentiles more than over the Jews, because few of the Jews believed and the rest persecuted Christianity.

13.12.0.en: After this severe rebuking speech from Samuel to King Saul, Samuel left Gilgal for Gibeah of Benjamin, angry and sorrowful at and for Saul, who by his foolishness lost everything. As for Saul, he numbered the people who remained with him and found them very few, six hundred men, who were of course unable to face the Philistines.

13.12.1.en: Do not rush in speech or action without asking God and thinking calmly, lest you break His commandments, wrong others and lose many blessings.

13.12.2.en: (3) The movement of the Philistine army (vv. 16-23): 16 And Saul, and Jonathan his son, and the people that were present with them, abode in Gibeah of Benjamin: but the Philistines encamped in Michmash. 17 And the spoilers came out of the camp of the Philistines in three companies: one company turned unto the way that leadeth to Ophrah, unto the land of Shual: 18 And another company turned the way to Beth-horon: and another company turned to the way of the border that looketh to the valley of Zeboim toward the wilderness. 19 Now there was no smith found throughout all the land of Israel: for the Philistines said, Lest the Hebrews make them swords or spears: 20 But all the Israelites went down to the Philistines, to sharpen every man his plowshare, and his sickle, and his axe, and his mattock, 21 when the edges of the plowshares and the sickles and the three-toothed forks and the axes had become dull, and to set the goads. 22 So it came to pass in the day of battle, that there was neither sword nor spear found in the hand of any of the people that were with Saul and Jonathan: but with Saul and with Jonathan his son was there found. 23 And the garrison of the Philistines went out to the passage of Michmash.

13.13.0.en: After the new circumstances, Saul was compelled to join his son Jonathan in an attempt to unite efforts. We understand from this that he left “Michmash,” which had been his base before (v. 2) and was now a high base for the Philistines, and Gibeah of Benjamin was also a high base for Saul, his son and their men, and between the two places was a low, deep valley.

13.14.1.en: Shual: about 6 km east of Bethel.

13.14.2.en: Beth-horon: about 19 km north of Jerusalem.

13.14.3.en: There were three roads going out from Michmash: the first to the north, heading toward the land of Shual, which was in the portion of the tribe of Benjamin; the second road to the west, heading to the town of Beth-horon, which was in the portion of Benjamin and Ephraim; and the last road to the east, heading toward the wilderness of the Jordan. So the Philistines divided themselves into three groups like highwaymen, ruling and plundering all the Israelite villages along the three roads going out from Michmash. They would seize the crops and impose tolls for passing along these roads, so the children of Israel were in great distress. Also, the Philistines’ movement and their control of the northern and central region isolated Saul in the southern region, and a narrow, deep valley separated him from them. Despite this devastation and the severe distress that befell the children of Israel, God’s mercy appears in that He allowed the Philistines to carry out this devastation so that the people would repent and return to God, because if the Philistines had fought Saul and those with him and prevailed over them at Gilgal, they would have occupied the lands of all the tribes of the children of Israel. This shows that God let the Philistines stray from destroying His people and be occupied with the idea of blocking the road to Saul and not strike him directly, although this would have been easy for them. For God leads your enemies astray until you repent and return to Him, and then you prevail over them, as happened with Jonathan and Saul (ch. 14).

13.15.0.en: The Philistines were able to close all the blacksmith workshops and forbade every craftsman in Israel from practicing his trade, so that the Israelites would not be able to make the weapons their army needed, swords or spears.

13.16.0.en: To sharpen: to whet the iron.

13.16.1.en: His plowshare: the iron of the plow that cuts the earth.

13.16.2.en: The mattock: like the axe but with a larger head, and used with rocks.

13.16.3.en: The misery and humiliation of the people reached their height, for they resorted to the Philistines’ blacksmith workshops in order to be able to sharpen the farming tools, the sickle, the plow, the axe and the mattock, after the Philistines had closed all the workshops of the children of Israel.

13.17.0.en: Dull: wearied, and it comes here in the sense of having lost its sharpness.

13.17.1.en: Plowshares: plural of plowshare, the iron of the plow.

13.17.2.en: Three-toothed forks: three metal teeth with a long handle, like a fork (the pitchfork). To set the goads: that is, fixing the metal pieces onto the wooden handles in all the farming tools mentioned above.

13.17.3.en: This verse is entirely connected with the preceding one, for it completes the meaning that the Israelites were not permitted to sharpen their farming tools when they became worn with age and needed sharpening.

13.18.0.en: To show the bad condition of the men gathered with Saul and his son Jonathan, it explains that none of them carried a weapon except Saul and his son, because of the people’s distance from God and Saul’s pride. This is a symbol that when a person moves away from God he loses the spiritual weapons with which he overcomes Satan.

13.19.0.en: The garrison: they are the vanguard of the army, or what are called reconnaissance units.

13.19.1.en: The Philistines became still bolder and sent men from among them to the passage of Michmash, which is a narrow pass governed and bounded by two great rocks, and whoever controls this pass tightens his grip on Michmash and is able to set out from it to other places. That is, the Philistines took control of the road to the city of Michmash and beyond it.

13.19.2.en: Satan tries to strip you of your spiritual weapons and make you depend on the desires of the world, just as the Philistines made the children of Israel depend on them for sharpening their weapons and farming tools. But you, as a spiritual person, rely on God and do not indulge in material desires; rather, use everything in measure, and depend for your strength on God and not on passing material things, and the devil will not be able to humble you. The victory over the Philistines
